documents.unit: Office of the Provost, Teaching Support and Innovation
documents.title: AI at UO: Statement of Purpose, Policy FAQ and course-policy guidance
documents.summary: The Provost-level page gives a statement of purpose, baseline instructor duties (a syllabus AI statement, the need for a conduct finding before an AI-related grade penalty) and three sample stances. It also summarizes the AI Council's 18 recommendations and a faculty Year of Action.
documents.stance_why: The page says syllabus policy is "decided at your own or your unit's discretion" and offers three broad stances (Not Allowed, Allowed With Limits, Allowed No Limits), so the university sets no default and hands the choice to instructors; tiers are listed.

units.why: The purpose statement is the institution-wide principle for AI in teaching: "adopt AI purposefully to enhance the human capacity for ethical, critical, and creative thinking". It is a framework statement for everyone, so I chose P56 (institution-level purpose and principles), phase general, modality informs.
units.anchor: adopt AI purposefully to enhance the human capacity for ethical, critical, and creative thinking
units.frag_start: True to our liberal arts core

units.why: The FAQ says "Have a syllabus policy statement on what AI use is allowed", a baseline duty on instructors to state AI expectations, so P09 fits; it is a before-course design duty and a must.
units.anchor: Have a syllabus policy statement on what AI use is allowed
units.frag_end: revise them as needed to protect assessment integrity.

units.why: The same sentence says the policy is "decided at your own or your unit's discretion", so the university does not set the stance and leaves it to the instructor. P04 is the instructor-level delegation; P85 (units) would also fit, but the instructor is named first, so P04.
units.anchor: decided at your own or your unit
units.frag_end: revise them as needed to protect assessment integrity.
units.policy: Instructors decide what AI use is allowed, at their own or their unit's discretion.
units.fit_note: The unit-level discretion is also named (P85).

units.why: The decision is to be made "based on the course's learning objectives", tying AI permission to learning goals, which is exactly P83.
units.anchor: based on the course's learning objectives
units.frag_end: revise them as needed to protect assessment integrity.

units.why: Instructors must "Stay aware of how well AI can complete your assignments and exams and revise them as needed", a duty to redesign assessments around AI, so P35; stated as a baseline responsibility, a should.
units.anchor: revise them as needed to protect assessment integrity
units.frag_end: revise them as needed to protect assessment integrity.

units.why: A grade penalty "requires a formal finding from the Office of Student Conduct and Community Standards first". This is a procedural rule for instructors suspecting AI misuse, so P81 (formal reporting procedure) fits better than P36 because it governs steps rather than classification.
units.anchor: requires a formal finding from the Office of Student Conduct and Community Standards first
units.frag_start: You can always grade against your criteria

units.why: "You can ask students to use AI through UO-approved systems" tells instructors they may require AI use in coursework, which is P79 (instructors may require it).
units.anchor: You can ask students to use AI
units.frag_start: You can ask students to use AI
units.policy: Instructors may ask students to use AI in assigned work through UO-approved systems.

units.why: The page names the tools that count as approved: "Copilot Chat with data protection", plus AI features built into course platforms. These are institution-approved tools, so P92 rather than P17 (course-specific).
units.anchor: Copilot Chat with data protection
units.frag_start: You can ask students to use AI
units.policy: UO-approved systems for assigned AI use are Copilot Chat with data protection and AI features built into existing course platforms (e.g., ALEKS in Math, Westlaw CoCounsel in Law).

units.why: With approved tools "students don't need separate accounts with outside vendors", which protects cost and data exposure; P50 (vetted tools, data protection) fits.
units.anchor: separate accounts with outside vendors
units.policy: With UO-approved tools, students do not need separate accounts with outside vendors.

units.why: If a tool needs a third-party account, the instructor must "provide the possibility to opt out", an equity and access safeguard so P51.
units.anchor: provide the possibility to opt out
units.frag_start: If you're teaching with a tool

units.why: The instructor "must consider the security, accessibility, and cost of these tools" before assigning a third-party tool. This is assessing a tool before choosing it, P117; it is not institutional approval (P65).
units.anchor: you must consider the security, accessibility, and cost of these tools
units.frag_start: If you're teaching with a tool

units.why: "Every UO syllabus should say something about GenAI" is a syllabus-statement requirement, P09; should since it is stated as an expectation.
units.anchor: Every UO syllabus should say something about GenAI.

units.why: "It names what students can learn from working with AI, or from working without it" asks that the policy be tied to a learning objective, P83.
units.anchor: It names what students can learn from working with AI, or from working without it

units.why: "Students move between courses with very different AI policies" is a fact about differing policies, close to P11 (each course governs itself), but it only informs and does not state a binding rule.
units.anchor: Students move between courses with very different AI policies.
units.fit_note: States the fact of varying course policies as the reason for transparency; it does not say one course's rule does not carry over.

units.why: "Say what's allowed on the syllabus and in assignment instructions, and be ready to explain your reasoning if asked" asks instructors to be transparent and explain reasons; P66 (explain rules) fits, and P09 is secondary.
units.anchor: be ready to explain your reasoning if asked

units.why: Defines the "Not Allowed" tier: "Students may not use AI tools to produce course materials or assignments, in whole or part." It is one of three named stances, so P05 (named tiers).
units.anchor: Students may not use AI tools to produce course materials or assignments
units.frag_start: Students may not use AI tools
units.policy: Tier "Not Allowed": students may not use AI tools to produce course materials or assignments, in whole or part.

units.why: Defines the "Allowed, With Limits" tier: "Certain tasks or tools are permitted; others aren't, or require citation". Named tier, P05.
units.anchor: Certain tasks or tools are permitted
units.policy: Tier "Allowed, With Limits": certain tasks or tools are permitted; others are not, or require citation and documentation of use.

units.why: Defines the "Allowed, No Limits" tier: "AI is open for use across the course, typically still with a citation expectation". Named tier, P05.
units.anchor: AI is open for use across the course
units.policy: Tier "Allowed, No Limits": AI is open for use across the course, typically still with a citation expectation.

units.why: "students need to see AI expectations at the assignment level, not just the course level" asks instructors to state expectations on each assignment, a communication rule closest to P09 but extending it to assignments.
units.anchor: students need to see AI expectations at the assignment level, not just the course level
units.fit_note: Extends the syllabus-statement duty to assignment-level statements.

units.why: "Research suggests students need to see AI expectations" cites research as the basis for the guidance, evidence about learning, P55; the page does not give the data itself.
units.anchor: Research suggests students need to see AI expectations at the assignment level
units.fit_note: Cites research only in passing as a basis for assignment-level statements.

units.why: "Our AI-aware assignment template" supplies a template for instructors to carry policy into assignments, i.e. templates for instructors, P110.
units.anchor: Our AI-aware assignment template can help you carry your policy into individual assignments.

units.why: "Communicate your rationale, not just the rule" asks instructors to give students the reasons for their AI rules, P66.
units.anchor: Communicate your rationale, not just the rule.

units.why: The Council's approach is "both embracing AI tools to prepare students for their careers and futures", a career-readiness reason to learn AI, P44.
units.anchor: both embracing AI tools to prepare students for their careers and futures

units.why: The same sentence adds "deepening the human skills and relationships that give a liberal arts education its enduring value", a stated priority to protect human skills. No type captures it exactly: not P41 (practice builds skill) or P121 (displacement), so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: deepening the human skills and relationships that give a liberal arts education its enduring value
units.uncovered_note: The university commits to deepening human skills and relationships as a counterweight to AI.

units.why: "18 GenAI in Teaching and Learning recommendations, endorsed by the AI Council August 19, 2026" states who made and adopted the recommendations and when, P84.
units.anchor: endorsed by the AI Council
units.policy: 18 GenAI in Teaching and Learning recommendations were endorsed by the AI Council on August 19, 2026.

units.why: The recommendations aim to move "from individual, ad hoc responses to GenAI toward more systematic ones", a framework statement of direction, P56.
units.anchor: shifts us from individual, ad hoc responses to GenAI toward more systematic ones

units.why: One advancement is to "ensure faculty set clear course policies on AI use, receive feedback on their approaches", an institutional aim to require clear course policies, closest to P09 but also covering feedback and evaluation.
units.anchor: ensure faculty set clear course policies on AI use, receive feedback on their approaches
units.fit_note: Also says faculty receive feedback and that adaptation work is made visible in evaluation.

units.why: "confirming that grades reflect real learning" is a goal about honest, valid evaluation under AI; P95 (honest evaluation) is nearest, though it is not framed as fairness.
units.anchor: confirming that grades reflect real learning
units.fit_note: Frames the goal as grades reflecting real learning and keeping taught skills meaningful, not as fairness to peers.

units.why: The third advancement says UO will "boldly signal ... that UO is evolving in light of AI", an institution-level positioning statement, P56.
units.anchor: UO is evolving in light of AI and that we teach the durable human skills

units.why: "Build your own AI literacy in conversation with expert colleagues" offers faculty learning opportunities (Year of Action), P63.
units.anchor: Build your own AI literacy

units.why: "Stipended faculty-led spaces: AI Literacy, Unit-level Support, Educational Research, Writing in the Age of AI" are communities of practice for faculty, P63.
units.anchor: Stipended faculty-led spaces

units.why: The Teaching Day of Exchange features "strategies for both integrating AI and motivating meaningful student work without it", a faculty sharing event, P63.
units.anchor: strategies for both integrating AI and motivating meaningful student work without it

units.why: Faculty are invited to "Help shape institutional direction", including "researching student views"; inviting input and research on student views, P55 is nearest.
units.anchor: researching student views
units.fit_note: Invites faculty to research student views and help define AI literacy, i.e. participation in shaping policy.

documents.unit: Office of the Provost, Teaching Support and Innovation
documents.title: AI & Academic Integrity
documents.summary: Teaching-center guidance on AI and academic integrity. It notes the Code's plagiarism definition covers uncited AI, that UO does not support detectors, and that grade penalties for suspected misconduct require a finding by the conduct office.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no rule on whether AI may be used; it describes the conduct code definition, detector limits and the reporting process ("handled by the Office of Student Conduct and Community Standards"), leaving use decisions to instructors.

units.why: "updated the 'Ducks Have Integrity' module that all incoming students take to include AI" is an AI-integrity training for students, P70.
units.anchor: that all incoming students take to include AI

units.why: The module update also aims to "bolster students' confidence in asking instructors about appropriate use", encouraging students to ask; P10.
units.anchor: confidence in asking instructors about appropriate use

units.why: The Student Conduct Code says plagiarism "may include artificial intelligence (AI) content generators and generative AI tools" when use is not cited, classing uncited AI use as misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: may include artificial intelligence (AI) content generators and generative AI tools

units.why: "UO does not currently support AI detection tools" says the university does not endorse detectors, P39.
units.anchor: UO does not currently support AI detection tools

units.why: Detectors "may not be effective and can result in false positives", an unreliability statement, P39.
units.anchor: may not be effective and can result in false positives

units.why: Percentages from detectors are not "dispositive on their own", a standard for evidence of misuse, P69.
units.anchor: we would not consider the percentages provided by these tools as dispositive on their own

units.why: Updates to the Code "now require all suspected academic misconduct cases that include a grade penalty be handled by the Office of Student Conduct", a required procedure, P81.
units.anchor: require all suspected academic misconduct cases that include a grade penalty be handled by

units.why: "instructors should not impose a grade penalty without a finding from that office" limits instructor sanctions, P81 (procedure).
units.anchor: instructors should not impose a grade penalty without a finding from that office

units.why: Instructors submit the report "within five business days of discovery", a reporting procedure with a deadline, P81.
units.anchor: within five business days of discovery

units.why: "Contact SCCS with questions about academic integrity" points instructors to a support office, P115.
units.anchor: Contact SCCS with questions about academic integrity

documents.unit: Office of the Dean of Students
documents.title: Student Conduct Updates for Faculty (plagiarism definition and ChatGPT guidance)
documents.summary: A 2023 Dean of Students letter to faculty on conduct changes: AI-generated material counts as plagiarism, misconduct with grade penalties goes to the conduct office, and detector scores are not proof. It suggests detection methods and urges instructors to set and discuss AI expectations.
documents.stance_why: The letter encourages faculty to "consider and determine your own course philosophy and expectations" per course and sets no stance of its own; it defines plagiarism to include AI and explains conduct procedure.

units.why: The Trustees changed the Code so "any academic misconduct concerns" with a possible grade penalty are "adjudicated by SCCS", a formal-procedure rule, P81.
units.anchor: adjudicated by SCCS where a grade penalty may result from a violation

units.why: The change is justified by ensuring "the protections and rights embedded in the formal student conduct process are afforded to students", a student-rights rationale; P64 is nearest but this is not an explicit right to respond.
units.anchor: the protections and rights embedded in the formal student conduct process are afforded to students
units.fit_note: States student protections in the conduct process generally, without naming a right to respond.

units.why: "You retain the ability to resolve academic misconduct concerns informally" lets instructors handle cases themselves. No type covers informal resolution, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: You retain the ability to resolve academic misconduct concerns informally
units.uncovered_note: Instructors may resolve academic misconduct concerns informally without a formal case.

units.why: Even without a grade penalty, "we encourage you to utilize the Reporting Academic Misconduct Form to submit incidents", a reporting step, P81.
units.anchor: to submit incidents for our review

units.why: The formal process "allows us to have educational conversations with students about academic misconduct", treating misuse as educative, P68.
units.anchor: have educational conversations with students about academic misconduct

units.why: "SCCS maintains records about any prior or future violations by a student" keeps records to identify patterns. No type covers record keeping, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: SCCS maintains records about any prior or future violations by a student
units.uncovered_note: The conduct office keeps records of prior violations to address patterns of behavior.

units.why: "Plagiarism also includes the submission of material generated by others" bars submitting others' generated work as one's own, P19; the AI examples follow in the next sentence.
units.anchor: Plagiarism also includes the submission of material generated by others.

units.why: The next sentence lists AI generators such as ChatGPT as examples of material generated by others, classifying such submission as plagiarism, P36.
units.anchor: artificial intelligence (AI) content generators and generative AI tools such as ChatGPT
units.policy: Submitting material from AI content generators and generative AI tools such as ChatGPT can be plagiarism under the Student Conduct Code.

units.why: "I encourage you to incorporate these definitions into your course syllabus and in discussions with students" asks instructors to put misconduct definitions in syllabi, P09, with discussion as secondary.
units.anchor: incorporate these definitions into your course syllabus and in discussions with students

units.why: "Allegations of plagiarism involving the use of generative AI tools have constituted over half of all academic misconduct reports" is a data point about AI and misconduct, P55.
units.anchor: have constituted over half of all academic misconduct reports

units.why: The Dean joins the Provost "in encouraging all faculty to consider and determine your own course philosophy and expectations around the use of generative AI tools for each of your courses", leaving the rule to each instructor, P04.
units.anchor: determine your own course philosophy and expectations around the use of generative AI tools

units.why: Instructors should "communicate those expectations in your course syllabus", a syllabus-statement expectation, P09.
units.anchor: communicate those expectations in your course syllabus

units.why: Instructors should "discuss them in the first week of the term", i.e. talk through the AI expectations in class, P66.
units.anchor: discuss them in the first week of the term

units.why: "Sample course syllabus language can be found at teaching.uoregon.edu/ai" provides sample syllabus statements, P110.
units.anchor: Sample course syllabus language can be found at

units.why: If AI is prohibited, "running your specific assignment prompt through a generative AI tool" and comparing with student work is offered as a detection method, P40.
units.anchor: Running your specific assignment prompt through a generative AI tool one or more times

units.why: The letter says AI work "typically" contains "similar inaccuracies" and suggests checking for fabricated information as evidence, P40.
units.anchor: a propensity to include factually inaccurate or otherwise fabricated information

units.why: "Comparing the assignment of concern with other work submitted by the student" for style changes is a process-evidence check, P40.
units.anchor: looking for distinct and significant changes in writing style

units.why: "Verifying quotes, sources, and citations" is offered because AI "may fabricate these", another detection method, P40.
units.anchor: Verifying quotes, sources, and citations used in the assignment.

units.why: "Writing your assignment prompts in a manner that makes generative AI use more obvious" is an assignment-design response to AI, P35.
units.anchor: Writing your assignment prompts in a manner that makes generative AI use more obvious

units.why: "online AI detection tools ... may not be effective and can result in false positives" says detectors are unreliable, P39.
units.anchor: may not be effective and can result in false positives
units.frag_start: The University of Oregon has determined

units.why: "we would not consider the percentages provided by these tools as dispositive on their own" sets an evidence standard, P69.
units.anchor: we would not consider the percentages provided by these tools as dispositive on their own

units.why: "You may use these tools and the percentages generated by them as a starting point" permits detector output as one factor, P40.
units.anchor: as a starting point, or an additional factor

units.why: "without any additional information or an acknowledgement from the student ... there may not be enough to find that they engaged in a violation" sets what evidence is needed for a finding, P69.
units.anchor: there may not be enough to find that they engaged in a violation

units.why: "We can still have educational conversations with students even when there is not enough information to find a violation" is an educative response, P68.
units.anchor: We can still have educational conversations with students
units.frag_start: We can still have educational conversations
units.frag_end: for review when you have concerns about potential academic misconduct.

units.why: "we encourage you to continue to refer these cases to SCCS for review" asks instructors to report even when evidence is thin, P81.
units.anchor: continue to refer these cases to SCCS for review

units.why: The Student Conduct Code changes are proposed by the Student Conduct Advisory Committee of "students, staff, and faculty" and approved by the Board, which describes how the policy was made, P84.
units.anchor: changes to the Student Conduct Code proposed by the Student Conduct Advisory Committee

notes: No school or computing-unit documents in the collect file. The DOS letter repeats some conduct-procedure content from the integrity page; each document is coded on its own.
